questions.question_text: Which protected class does Oregon fair housing law cover that federal law does NOT?
distractors: Race
Familial status
National origin
questions.explanation: Oregon adds source of income to the housing protections, which federal law does not cover (ORS 659A.421). Race, familial status and national origin are all federally protected under the Fair Housing Act.

questions.question_text: A tenant applies with a Section 8 voucher. The landlord refuses, citing a preference for traditional income. Under Oregon law, this is:
distractors: Legal if applied uniformly to all applicants
Legal because vouchers are voluntary
Permitted if disclosed in the listing
questions.explanation: Source of income is defined to include federal rent subsidy payments under 42 U.S.C. 1437f and other local, state or federal housing assistance (ORS 659A.421). Refusing an applicant because rent comes from a voucher is unlawful.

questions.question_text: An Oregon landlord rejects an applicant whose income is child support and alimony. Does this violate Oregon's source-of-income protection?
questions.correct_answer: No, the protection covers housing assistance, not private income
distractors: Yes, all lawful income sources are protected
Yes, but only if the applicant also holds a voucher
No, because landlords may set any income rule they choose
questions.explanation: Oregon defines source of income as federal rent subsidies under 42 U.S.C. 1437f and other local, state or federal housing assistance (ORS 659A.421). Child support and alimony fall outside that definition, so refusing them is not source-of-income discrimination.

questions.question_text: Oregon fair housing complaints are administered by the:
distractors: Oregon Real Estate Agency
Oregon Department of Justice
Oregon Housing Authority
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Division of the Bureau of Labor and Industries handles Oregon fair housing complaints. A complainant may also go to HUD or file a private lawsuit instead.

questions.question_text: An Oregon landlord advertises 'traditional families preferred.' This likely violates protections for which TWO classes?
distractors: Race and national origin
Religion and sex
Disability and source of income
questions.explanation: 'Traditional families preferred' signals a preference based on family composition and on being married, and Oregon protects both familial status and marital status (ORS 659A.421). Stating such a preference in an advertisement is itself discriminatory.

questions.question_text: An Oregon tenant who uses a wheelchair asks to install grab bars in the bathroom. What does Oregon fair housing law require of the landlord?
questions.correct_answer: Permit the modification at the tenant's expense
distractors: Pay for and install the grab bars
Deny the request if the lease bars alterations
Move the tenant to an accessible unit instead
questions.explanation: A housing provider may not refuse a reasonable modification of the premises made at the disabled individual's expense (ORS 659A.145). The landlord may require the tenant to restore the interior afterward, apart from normal wear and tear.

questions.question_text: A rental has a strict no-pets policy. An applicant who is blind uses a guide dog. What must the landlord do?
questions.correct_answer: Make a reasonable accommodation in the policy
distractors: Charge a pet deposit for the animal
Enforce the no-pets policy uniformly
Require the change at the tenant's expense
questions.explanation: Refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules or policies needed for equal enjoyment of a dwelling is unlawful discrimination (ORS 659A.145). An assistance animal is not a pet, so waiving the no-pets rule is the accommodation and no pet deposit applies.

questions.question_text: An Oregon homeowner rents a bedroom inside the house she lives in and shares the kitchen with the tenant. Does ORS 659A.421 govern her tenant selection?
questions.correct_answer: No, an owner-occupied shared-space residence is exempt
distractors: Yes, Oregon recognizes no housing exemptions
Only the source-of-income provision applies
Yes, unless she hires a licensed broker
questions.explanation: Oregon exempts an owner-occupied single-family residence the owner keeps as a primary residence where occupants share common space (ORS 659A.421). Outside that narrow carve-out the statute reaches essentially every rental and sale in the state.

questions.question_text: An Oregon community limits residency to people 55 and older. Is that age restriction lawful?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, qualifying housing for older persons is exempt
distractors: No, age is a protected class in Oregon housing law
Only if the community receives federal subsidy
Only for communities restricted to age 62 and older
questions.explanation: Housing that qualifies as housing for older persons is exempt from the familial status provisions (ORS 659A.421). The community has to actually meet the occupancy and program conditions for the 55-and-over or 62-and-over category it claims.

questions.question_text: A buyer's agent submits a personal letter from the buyer along with the offer. What must the seller's agent do under current Oregon law?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing special — the 2021 ban no longer applies
distractors: Reject the letter and refuse to transmit it
Transmit it only after redacting protected characteristics
Report the buyer's agent to OREA
questions.explanation: HB 2550 (2021) once made seller's agents reject buyer communications beyond customary documents, but a federal court enjoined it on First Amendment grounds and HB 4063 (2024) struck it from ORS 696.805. Fair housing law still limits how a seller may act on what the letter reveals.

questions.question_text: A person believes they were denied housing in Oregon due to their race. Where can they file a complaint?
questions.correct_answer: Oregon Civil Rights Division, HUD, or court
distractors: Only with HUD at the federal level
Only through the Oregon Real Estate Agency
Only by filing a private lawsuit
questions.explanation: Oregon fair housing complainants have three avenues: filing with the Oregon Civil Rights Division at the state level, filing with HUD at the federal level, or pursuing a private lawsuit in court.

questions.question_text: Which remedy is available in an Oregon fair housing complaint?
distractors: Criminal imprisonment only
License revocation only
Mandatory property forfeiture
questions.explanation: Oregon fair housing remedies include actual damages, injunctive relief, and civil penalties. Criminal imprisonment and property forfeiture are not standard remedies in fair housing enforcement.

questions.question_text: A landlord charges higher rent to tenants using housing vouchers. If found liable, which outcome is MOST likely?
questions.correct_answer: Payment of actual damages and civil penalties
distractors: A warning letter with no financial penalty
Mandatory sale of the rental property
Automatic license suspension for one year
questions.explanation: Charging more because rent comes from a voucher is source-of-income discrimination, and Oregon remedies run to actual damages plus civil penalties (ORS 659A.421). Differential pricing is treated the same as an outright refusal.

questions.question_text: A complainant wins a fair housing case through the Oregon Civil Rights Division. The respondent must pay damages but continues the discriminatory practice. What additional remedy applies?
questions.correct_answer: Injunctive relief ordering the practice to stop
distractors: The case is automatically dismissed
Only further monetary fines are available
The complainant must refile with HUD
questions.explanation: Injunctive relief is a court order requiring the respondent to cease the discriminatory practice. It is available in addition to actual damages and civil penalties under Oregon fair housing law.

questions.question_text: An Oregon tenant files a fair housing complaint with HUD instead of the state. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, complainants may choose either venue
distractors: No, state complaints must go to the state first
Only if the state agency declines jurisdiction
Only for federally protected classes
questions.explanation: Oregon fair housing complainants are not required to file at the state level first. They may file with the Oregon Civil Rights Division, HUD, or pursue a private lawsuit, and these options are not mutually exclusive.
